## The Superior National Forest wolf study

Beginning in the late 1960s, L. David Mech and colleagues with the U.S. Geological Survey radio-tracked wolves in the Superior National Forest of northeastern Minnesota, one of the longest-running wolf studies anywhere (Mech 2009, 2022; Barber-Meyer et al. 2021). It included some of the earliest radio-collaring of wolf pups. This poster revisits 139 of those pups, collared from 1970 to 2017, to ask when and how they died, how many survived their first two years, and what factors shaped their survival.

## At a glance

::: {.glance}
<div><b>62%</b><span>survived their first year after capture (46% to 2 years)</span></div>
<div><b>25 of 51</b><span>deaths were caused by people</span></div>
<div><b>7 of 7</b><span>starvation or disease deaths came before age 1</span></div>
<div><b>November</b><span>deadliest month: 18 of 51 deaths, including 7 of 9 shootings</span></div>
:::

## Methods in brief

- **Study area.** Superior National Forest, northeastern Minnesota, USA. Pups radio-collared by the USGS Wolf and Deer Project, 1970 to 2017.
- **Pups.** 343 pup captures. 150 pups were collared once, caught between 22 June and 15 November, with a known monitoring history. The 11 deaths linked to capture or the collar were removed, leaving 139 pups.
- **Fates.** 51 pups died while monitored. 88 were censored at last contact: they dispersed, their signal was lost, their collar came off or failed, or monitoring ended. Pups that dispersed and were later found dead count as censored at last contact.
- **Causes.** Four groups: human-caused (25), starvation or disease (7), wolves or other wildlife (3), and cause unknown (16). A cause recorded only as "possible" or "probable" counts as unknown.
- **Survival.** Kaplan-Meier survival from the day of capture, and cumulative incidence of each cause (R package `survival`).
- **Cox models.** One cause-specific Cox model per cause group, on pup age (all pups assumed born 15 April; each pup enters at the age it was caught). Predictors were weight compared with what is expected for a pup of its sex caught on that date, and road density within 5 km of the capture site. Standard errors are clustered by litter; 134 pups had both predictors.

### The 25 human-caused deaths

12 were illegal (7 shot, 5 trapped or snared), 7 were accidental (6 hit by a vehicle or snowmobile, 1 caught by a fox trapper), 2 were legal (1 trapped in 1973, 1 in the 2013 harvest), and 4 had no legality recorded.

## Figures

::: {.plate}
![](figs/map.jpg){fig-alt="Map of the study area around Ely, Minnesota, showing all 139 pups at their capture sites."}
:::
**Fig. 1.** Pups were caught across the study area, both inside and outside the Boundary Waters Wilderness (shaded green). Each dot marks one pup's capture site and is coloured by cause of death (51 pups) or by how monitoring ended (88 pups). Thin rings mark pups that reached 1 year old, and thick rings mark those that reached 2 years, labelled with estimated age at death or last contact, and sex.

::: {.plate}
![](figs/histories.jpg){fig-alt="One line per pup from age at capture to death or last contact, coloured by fate."}
:::
**Fig. 2.** Of the 51 deaths, 41 occurred before age 1. Each line follows one pup from its age at capture to its age at death (dot) or last contact, coloured by fate. The dashed line shows that every pup had been caught by 6.8 months of age.

::: {.plate}
![](figs/fates.jpg){fig-alt="Stacked bars of how monitoring ended and the 51 deaths by cause."}
:::
**Fig. 3.** People caused half of all deaths. The top bar shows how monitoring ended for 139 pups: 51 died, and 88 dispersed, lost signal, or lost their collar. The bottom bar breaks the 51 deaths down by cause. The 11 pups that died from capture or collar-related causes are not included.

::: {.plate}
![](figs/calendar.jpg){fig-alt="Deaths per 100 pup-months by calendar month and cause, peaking in November."}
:::
**Fig. 4.** Deaths peaked in November, at the start of hunting and trapping seasons. Bars show deaths per 100 pup-months (one pup tracked for one month), which accounts for more pups being monitored in some months than others. Numbers above the bars are deaths, and numbers below the months are pup-months monitored. April to June bars include only pups in their second year.

::: {.plate}
![](figs/km.jpg){fig-alt="Kaplan-Meier survival curve over 36 months since capture."}
:::
**Fig. 5.** Survival fell fastest in the first 3 months after capture, to 73%, and then levelled off. The solid line is the Kaplan-Meier estimate for 139 pups, and dotted lines show the 95% confidence interval. Ticks mark pups whose monitoring ended without a known death, and numbers below show how many pups were still monitored.

::: {.plate}
![](figs/weight.jpg){fig-alt="Relative risk of starvation or disease and unknown-cause death falling with pup weight."}
:::
**Fig. 6.** Lighter pups were more likely to die of starvation, disease, or unknown causes. Zero on the x axis is the weight expected for a pup of the same sex caught on the same date; the median pup was about 1 lb below expected. A pup 10 lb lighter than expected had about 6 times the median pup's risk of starving. Lines show Cox model hazard ratios, shading shows the 95% confidence interval, and ticks mark each pup's weight.

::: {.plate}
![](figs/roads.jpg){fig-alt="Relative risk of a human-caused death rising with road density."}
:::
**Fig. 7.** Pups caught where roads were dense were more likely to be killed by people. The median road density was 0.94 km of road per km² within 5 km of capture. A pup caught where road density was 1.75 had about 2.7 times the median pup's risk. The line shows the Cox model hazard ratio, shading shows the 95% confidence interval, and ticks mark each pup's road density.

### Extra figures

#### Inside the data

What the 134 pups in the Cox models looked like on each predictor we tested (the 139 pups minus 5 with no capture weight), and how deaths were spread across the years.

::: {.plate}
![](figs/pred_roads.jpg){fig-alt="Dot plot of road density within 5 km of each pup's capture site, with the median and average marked and pups later killed by people highlighted."}
:::
**Roads.** Each dot is one pup, placed by the density of roads within 5 km of where it was caught (dots are spread up and down only so they don't overlap). The solid line marks the median pup (0.94 km of road per km²), the reference every road hazard ratio is compared to, and the dashed line marks the average (0.88). Seventeen pups had no mapped road within 5 km. Pups later killed by people were caught at a median of 1.40 km of road per km², compared with 0.85 for the other pups. These are today's roads, used as a stand-in for past road access.

::: {.plate}
![](figs/map_mortalities.jpg){fig-alt="Map of northeastern Minnesota showing where 51 monitored pups died, coloured by cause, each joined by a straight line to its capture site, with the Boundary Waters Wilderness shaded."}
:::
**Where pups died.** Death sites of the 51 pups that died while monitored, coloured by cause, each joined by a straight line to its capture site (not the route travelled). Black rings mark pups that reached 1 or 2 years old. Most pups died close to home, a median 6.7 km from capture. People caused 24 of 40 deaths of pups caught outside the Boundary Waters Wilderness, but only 1 of 11 inside it. Of the 25 human-caused deaths, 12 are recorded as illegal, 2 legal, 7 accidental (mostly vehicles), and 4 not recorded. Locations are accurate to about 400 to 800 m, and Wolf 285's death site is provisional.

::: {.plate}
![](figs/pred_weight.jpg){fig-alt="Weight at capture against capture date for females and males, with a line for expected weight and pups that later died of starvation, disease, or unknown causes highlighted."}
:::
**Body condition.** Each dot is one pup, by capture date and weight. The line is the expected weight for a pup of that sex caught on that date, fitted to all pups, and each pup's distance above or below the line is the weight measure used in the models. Pups that later died of starvation or disease were a median 7.7 lb below the line, pups that died of unknown causes 4.1 lb below, and pups with no recorded death 1.9 lb above.

::: {.plate}
![](figs/pred_sex.jpg){fig-alt="Bars showing 63 females, 28 of which died while monitored, and 71 males, 23 of which died."}
:::
**Sex.** Of 63 females, 28 died while monitored; of 71 males, 23 died. Sex showed no clear effect in the models.

::: {.plate}
![](figs/pred_pups_by_year.jpg){fig-alt="Bars of pups caught each year from 1970 to 2017, over shaded bands showing the wolves' federal legal status at capture."}
:::
**Capture year and legal status.** Pups caught each year, with shaded bands for the wolves' federal legal status at capture. The 24 pups caught from 1970 to 1973, before federal protection, were tested as a group for human-caused deaths and showed no clear difference. Few pups were collared after 2000. Capture year itself was not tested as a predictor.

::: {.plate}
![](figs/pred_decade_deaths.jpg){fig-alt="Stacked bars of the share of pups that died while monitored, by cause, for each decade of capture."}
:::
**Deaths by decade of capture.** The share of pups that died while monitored, by cause, for each decade in which they were caught. Labels give deaths out of pups caught that decade. The 2000s and 2010s rest on only 9 and 10 pups, so their bars move a lot with each death.

#### Kaplan–Meier results

Kaplan–Meier uses no predictors, so it has no diagram. These figures show how the survival estimate was made and how much it depends on the pups we lost track of.

::: {.plate}
![](figs/naive_vs_km.jpg){fig-alt="Survival at 30 days, 90 days, 6 months, 1 year and 2 years from Kaplan-Meier with confidence intervals and from the naive method, with the gap labelled at each milestone."}
:::
**Why the abstract's numbers changed.** Survival at each milestone from Kaplan–Meier (with 95% confidence intervals) and from the naive method used in the abstract, which drops pups whose fate we lost. On the same 139 pups, the gap grows with time: 16 percentage points at 1 year (62% vs 46%) and 29 at 2 years (46% vs 17%), because most pups we lost track of were lost in their first year.

::: {.plate}
![](figs/km_sensitivity.jpg){fig-alt="Four Kaplan-Meier survival curves over 36 months since capture: the primary analysis and three sensitivity versions."}
:::
**How much our choices matter.** Kaplan–Meier survival under the primary rules and three alternatives; shading is the primary curve's 95% confidence interval. One-year survival barely moves (57 to 62%). Two-year survival ranges from 30% to 55%, depending mostly on whether deaths found long after contact was lost are counted, and only 9 pups were still monitored at 2 years.

::: {.plate}
![](figs/lost_timing.jpg){fig-alt="Months from capture to last contact for dispersed, signal-lost, and collar-off pups, and bars of the calendar month of last contact."}
:::
**When we lost track of pups.** Months from capture to last contact (left) and the calendar month of last contact (right) for the 88 pups whose monitoring ended without a recorded death. Signal loss came at about the same time after capture as dispersal (median 6.0 vs 7.5 months), while collars that came off or failed did so early (median 0.9 months), which suggests many lost-signal pups may have dispersed.

::: {.plate}
![](figs/lost_age.jpg){fig-alt="Estimated age at last contact for dispersed, signal-lost, and collar-off pups, with the first and second birthdays marked."}
:::
**How old pups were when we lost track of them.** Estimated age at last contact, assuming mid-April births. Collars came off in the first autumn (median 6 months), while dispersal clustered around the first birthday (median 13 months), and lost signals did too (median 12 months).

#### Cox model results

::: {.plate}
![](figs/model_diagram.jpg){fig-alt="Diagram of the four cause-specific Cox models: body condition and roads each feed human-caused, starvation or disease, unknown, and wolves or wildlife deaths, with hazard ratios listed in each cause box."}
:::
**What we tested.** One Cox model per cause of death, each with the same two predictors: pup body condition (weight compared with what is expected for its sex and capture date) and road density within 5 km of the capture site. Solid coloured arrows show clear effects and grey dashed arrows show none; each box lists both hazard ratios per 1 standard deviation, with 95% confidence intervals. Lighter pups were more likely to die of starvation, disease, or unknown causes, and pups caught among more roads were more likely to be killed by people. Starvation or disease rests on only 7 deaths, and wolves or other wildlife (3 deaths) were too few to interpret. Sex and legal status were also tested in broader models of all deaths, human-caused deaths, and starvation, disease, and unknown deaths combined, with no clear effect.

::: {.plate}
![](figs/twopups.jpg){fig-alt="Predicted survival from 5 to 24 months for a light pup near many roads versus a heavy pup with no roads nearby."}
:::
**Weight and roads together.** Predicted chance that a pup alive at 5 months is still alive, from the four cause-specific Cox models. A light pup caught among many roads had a 39% chance (95% CI 19 to 54%) of being alive at 1 year; a heavy pup with no roads within 5 km, 89% (80 to 96%); a typical pup, about 69%. Light and heavy, and many and few roads, are the 10th and 90th percentiles of our pups. Shading shows 95% confidence intervals from 400 bootstrap samples of litters.

::: {.plate}
![](figs/forest.jpg){fig-alt="Hazard ratios per standard deviation of weight and road density for each cause of death."}
:::
**What each predictor did to each cause of death.** Hazard ratios per 1 standard deviation (8.65 lb of weight; 0.63 km of road per km²), with 95% confidence intervals. Grey marks show no clear effect. Wolves or other wildlife (3 deaths) were too few to estimate.

## Conclusion

Deaths came early: 43 of the 51 occurred within a year of capture (34 within three months), and 18 fell in November alone. People caused half of all deaths (25 of 51), followed by unknown causes (16), starvation or disease (7), and wolves or other wildlife (3). Overall, 62% of pups survived their first year after capture and 46% their second. Pups caught where roads were dense were more often killed by people, and lighter pups were more likely to starve or die of unknown causes. Only 3 collared pups were tracked during the 2012 to 2014 harvest seasons (1 killed legally), too few to test harvest effects. Accounting for pups lost from monitoring raised 1-year survival from our abstract's preliminary 43% to 62%.


## Credits and how it was made

- **Data.** Collected by the U.S. Geological Survey Wolf and Deer Project in the Superior National Forest, led by L. David Mech and Shannon Barber-Meyer. Many technicians, pilots, and volunteers captured and radio-tracked these pups from 1970 to 2017.
- **Analysis and poster.** Megan Petersohn.
- **Support.** U.S. Geological Survey (most of this work), UBC Okanagan (WEiRG), and Swamp Donkey Solutions.
- **Statistics.** R, with the `survival` package (Kaplan-Meier survival and Cox proportional hazards models).
- **Data and figures.** Python (pandas, NumPy, matplotlib), with the Questrial typeface and a colour-blind-checked palette.
- **Map.** ArcGIS Pro. Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness boundary from the USDA Forest Service; lakes and inset from Natural Earth; basemap from Esri and its data partners.
- **Poster design.** Canva, including design elements from Canva's library. Wolf illustrations from Adobe Stock, used under license: standing pup by [Nadiia](https://stock.adobe.com/contributor/211487462/nadiia) (#1855017249) and leaping wolf by [Zabi](https://stock.adobe.com/contributor/211723773/zabi) (#1506859098), both generated with AI.
- **Colour palette.** Inspired by two Georgia O'Keeffe paintings. The colours for how monitoring ended come from *Sky Above Clouds IV* (1965), which she painted from views out of airplane windows; most of these pups were tracked from the air, and how their monitoring ended often came down to whether a plane could still pick up their signal. The cause-of-death colours come from *Antelope* (1954), an antelope skull resting on the desert floor, where death and the land around it blend together.
- **AI assistance.** I used Claude, an AI assistant made by Anthropic, to help code and debug the analysis, check numbers against the dataset, and review my writing, including this page. I directed the analysis, made the analytical decisions, and reviewed all results and wording.
- **Place.** This research took place within the traditional, ancestral, and contemporary homelands of the Anishinaabe (Ojibwe) and Dakota Peoples, on lands ceded in the 1854 Treaty of La Pointe, where the Bois Forte, Grand Portage, and Fond du Lac Bands of Lake Superior Chippewa retain treaty rights.
